blocks.x: Could you give your full name first so we can identify the different voices when somebody hears the tape later to transcribe it? Well Bill, to tell you the truth, it may sound like a lie but the majority of the people downtown really called me Waldron.
They don't call me Frog. They're just musicians and it looks like lately they're beginning to call me more Frog than ever.
Yeah, I've only I guess heard it the last few years too. Your first name is Waldron and then the last name Joseph.
Waldron Clement Joseph.
Your middle name is Clement. Clement. Can you tell us just when you were born?
Yeah 1919, September the 12th.
And what part of town is it right here in New Orleans?
Yeah, yeah 7th Ward.
Yeah, in 7th Ward.
Yeah, in Roman and Columbus.
Roman and Columbus. Can you tell us anything about your family? If you had any other musicians in the family?

I did. Yeah, my father he was a bass player but he didn't play bass, you know, music. My oldest brother he was a drummer. Second brother, what he sang was Celestan, Ferdinand Joseph. Oh yes. Yeah, he sang this on Decker label, this My Josephine.
Oh yeah, sure, I remember.
Then I have another brother, he still plays, plays drums. He had a brother in the show business.
Is he older or younger?
Oh, they're all older now. I'm the last one.
You're the youngest one in the family. Did you say your father was a bass player?
Yeah.
String bass or kids or what did you say?

Yes, string bass. Matter of fact, I still had the bass. I think the bass, from what I could understand, the bass should be about nine or something, about nine years old. Probably a little better. Three strings, he made a four string out of it for me.
Oh, he had played three strings?
Yeah, he made a four string. Remember, Mr. Glenny used to have one. Yeah, well he was a friend with Mr. Glenny.
Can you tell us which bands he played with?
Oh no, no, no, no. I don't know if he had played with him. I really don't know, Bill.
How old were you when he died? He's dead now, I guess.
Yeah, when he died I was about, I say about, about twenty. No, no, no, no, I wasn't twenty, no, no Bill. I was about seventeen.
Seventeen. Yeah. So he would have died in the thirties then, long ago.

Yeah, over the thirties, yeah. But matter of fact, I had just started playing trombone professionally then. Yeah. Because see, I've been learning music ever since I was, well I say born, you see. Yeah. Because I had polio, and I was full of braces, so he bought all the instruments and put it at the house. So my first instrument was drum. I was studying drum music from Sister Cyril at Copper Crystal School. And, but he always wanted me to learn trombone. Well I did, in the meantime I would learn the trombone, drum and...
What did you, what was your very first instrument then?
Drums.
Drums was the very first.
Yeah, very first. And that was, you played that in the school band at Marcus Christie? Yeah, yeah.
I've heard about it, a few people have told us about that band. Was it just the regular during school hours or something extra outside?

Just school hours and then they used to have little concerts we used to play. Mm-hm. But I was playing drums in there. Yeah. I forget that. It wasn't no marching band, it was because we had violins and things like that. Yeah.

That's right, somebody did tell me about the string instruments. I forgot about it, who it was, told us about it. Yeah. Is there anything at all, I don't like to just keep pumping you about information on your father, because naturally I mean you couldn't remember, he probably didn't tell you everything about his life, but I was just I wondered, did he ever tell you anything when he started in music? How old was he too when he died?
Well I think my father was 54, 55 when he died.
Mm-hm.

By being the last one, you know, I mean, you wouldn't have all the information like the older boys, you know, like my brother Furtin' there, well he know all about that. Tell you the truth, he know a lot about this jazz business too. I mean a lot of it. He really knows. Nobody never, you know, talks to him.
By the way, do you have his address in mind, I mean, can you tell us where he lives and we'll make a note here on the tape so that we can, uh.
Oh he used to be 14, 1477 Northern Roman.
Seven, 1477 Northern Roman. Yeah well he, I tell you Bill, he'd be by the Union Hall all the time, you know the place where he'd be there.
Yeah, which are on the Esplanade.
No, Columbus.
Well, Columbus and, not Esplanade, Columbus and Cleveland.
Yeah, that's right. He know all about that.
Yeah, we'll have to talk to him too and he could probably get more information about that.

Well you see my daddy was a fellow like this, he loved music and he didn't want, and he had five boys and two girls, so his idea was just to put the instrument there, now who liked it take it, and who didn't. So I wound up liking it and I went through it lots of, you know, the right way.
When you started on drums did you have your own drum set at home?
Well my oldest brother, my oldest brother drum set. Yeah, my oldest brother.
Did you have to carry it back and forth to school with you?
Well they had, no, they had some drums at school, Sister Cyril had some drums at school, because I wasn't able to carry them in.
No, when you started on drums did you have a regular method then, or just in a class, or how did they teach you at the school?
Well, we was getting a group teaching and also we'd be taught in the middle, you know. Yeah, yeah.
Did you have a regular method, you had to learn to read and all?
Oh definitely, definitely, see, because in the meantime I was learning, I was going, my first teacher on trombone was Gene Ware, because I used to rehearse at the house with my brother, see.
Yeah.
And, well he's really, a fella really encouraged me to play trombone. Well then he went out on the road with Joe Robichaud, well then I went to Lesson, I pinched back two real a while.
Whatever happened to him, I never did know him.
Gene Ware? Yeah. He died, he died in Munson, Indiana.
Well he died up north then. Yeah. I never did know him and I just wondered if he was still living someplace else, you know, or. Yeah.

And then I went to Lesson at Pinchback Two-Role for a while, but still playing in the school band, drum. Then after, I don't know what happened to Two-Role, but then I went to Lesson by Eddie Pearson.
Oh yeah.
Uh huh.
Well how old were you when you started on your drums?

Well, Bill I tell you, I guess I was around about seven man, because my brother's starting up. See, oh I couldn't get to school too well. And, uh, my cousin, she was a teacher at Carpet Christie, but she used to come help me. Well you know like these days, if a kid had polio now, well they make it possible for you to go back as well as in Fort Worth, which we were poor, you know. Yeah. So when I was about, I'd say about ten, well that's when I started playing in the school band, but I did have an idea about it. Yeah. And I had a piano and all, I had everything to work with. Yeah, see, and, uh, I was doing pretty well.

Um, were there any other, uh, jazz musicians, that is the musicians that later became jazz musicians in your orchestra or band at school? Do you remember who else was in there, anybody else? Maybe some of the older kids too, or different ones who had become musicians?
Well, it really built that out, because remember one fella still playing, his name is Manuel Cruz. They had some other fellas, but they're not, uh, they're not like in it like I am.
Oh, by the way, is Manuel Cruz still around town? Yeah, he is. I haven't seen him for a long time, he used to play clarinet and play some trumpet too.
Well he was playing trumpet dance.
Yeah, I heard him play trumpet in the parade.

Yeah, because a lot of time him and I, well you see, Bourbon Street wasn't, uh, wasn't the street dance. No. Out here. Well I used to play piano with Manuel on a lot of gigs, see. I didn't know how to read the piano music, but I could read the cymbals, you know. I mean not fast enough. You could get the chords. Yeah, I can read all the cymbals no matter how they can, you see. But still, I was still learning trombones, see, because trombones wasn't in demand, see.
And how old were you when you switched over to trombone?
Well I was, I'd say 16 years old, between 15 and 16.
Did you ever play that in the school of Arkansas or were you about three of the school and you were?
But always wanted to play a funeral or parade like that but would never ever.
Yeah. And you remember your first job about on trombone? Well yeah I could.
Whose band it was? I don't remember the first job but I can tell you a funny job.
Yeah.

Well Mike Neal, Beau and I, and I forgot who the drummer was, trombone, bass, two and drum. We played a gig. Without a trumpet. Oh yeah, without a trumpet. Yeah, without a trumpet. See, I tell you, now that's one thing I remember what my dad always said, you know, is learn the melody to a tune, see. Then the amplifiers after. Yeah. Well I like, I had a lot of advantage because I mean, I did learn a little bit about the piano, you know. I learned the changes. But I always tried to play a melody to a tune. Always did.
Yeah that's one of the things most of the fellas in New Orleans tell us, that they try to always have that melody heard sometimes.

Yeah, but now Bill, this is the man's thing about this. Now, since this music got back, this New Orleans music got back, well I got to give credit to Paul Bobberman. That's the man that brought me in here. I didn't have much idea about it but I always liked it but I didn't have a chance to exercise it, you know. But Paul is the man. He's the man who really put me in this New Orleans jazz.
After that first, after you said it wasn't necessarily your first job with that one without a trumpet player, it wasn't a clarinet on the.
No, no, no, just a three piece of drum, bass, and who was the drum, I don't know, maybe Mac Neill probably, you know. But it was good, we was talking about that there the other night.
Did you stick to the melody most of the time or did you do variations too?
Well yeah, I amplified around the melody, you know, yeah.
Let the people know what's happening. What was the girl playing, string bass or?
Bass, bass tuba, one little small bass tuba.
Yeah, a bright tuba.

Yeah, a little small one, you know. Uh huh. Because at that particular time they had a little band that called a question, say the high hatter. And uh, he was playing bass too. They had a pretty nice band then. School boy. And uh, they had another little band I was playing with. But we wasn't great as them though. But Paul is the man. He is.

Um, I was gonna ask if you can, anytime, this doesn't have to be in any special order, if you think of anything about your father later on or the bands he played with that might come to your mind, you can just interrupt whatever we're talking about. You don't have any idea which bands he played with?
No, well I don't. Don't. Played with Solastain or anyone like that? Oh no, no, I don't believe, no, no. No. I know my oldest brother, he used to play with, used to gig around with, kiddin' in there.
Oh, excuse the interruption again, but what, since uh, we're trying to get as much of the older history of the older men as possible too. What was your father's first name?
Arthur, Arthur Joseph, yeah. Arthur Joseph. My brother, our oldest brother's name was after him, Arthur Joseph.
Yeah. We might come across some other musicians, some of the older men that can remember playing with him too, you know, and if we, and if we.

Well I tell you now, I tell you who could tell you a lot about my dad, I think. Cause I remember he used to come borrow the bass, but I was real small. But he was friends with my mom and my dad. Pajal. Oh yeah. Played with George. You know, drag, slow drag. Oh yeah. Yeah, well now he can tell you. Yeah, he knew all about it. Yeah, he knew all about it. Yeah, yeah. He knew all about it.
He had a three string bass then.
Yeah, three.
And then you converted it over to four.
He did. For me, yeah.
When did you pick up bass, after the trombone I guess?

No, no, I was, I was hitting at all of them at the same time. About the same time. Well just like I said, you know, I wasn't able to get out. Yeah, the whole house is full of instruments. Yeah, I wasn't able to get out so I just, I was hitting at all of them at the same time, you know.
So the trombone became your favorite then?
Oh definitely, yeah, yeah.
Who else did you study with besides Eddie Pearson, you told me someone else.
Well Gene Ware was the first man. Yeah. Then I got good enough after that, when Gene Ware left, well, I was the first trombone player at Joe Robichaux High.
You know who else Gene Ware played with? Anybody besides Robichaux that you can remember?
Oh yeah, he played with, played with Daz Dune, he played with Faith Marble. He was an artist Bill, definitely, he was an Auburn man, he definitely was an Auburn man.
I don't remember now if he made any records with Robichaux.
Yeah, yeah.
Was he on those records?
Yeah, yeah, yeah, yeah.
The vocalians they made in the early thirties, he would have been on those.
Yeah, yeah, he was on those. He was a good arranger too, a lot of people didn't know him. Well then I got back with, you know, running up and down the road, well he helped my a lot.
When he taught you, did you, do you remember the method you used or any certain books or what did he have you to write?

Yeah, I, it was, let's see, the first method. Matter of fact, I started my little ball off with one. It was white, let me see, white, white flamm or white something, I forgot to, I knew it was white something method.
There was a publisher called White or something in Boston.
Well it might be it Bill.
What excelsior methods?
White excelsior.
Maybe.
That's not like. Something like that.
Yeah, that's, that's.
I'm not sure either. Yeah, I'm quite sure that's it. White excelsior. Well they had my little boy, he was in the night, last week we got him in Auburn. He's doing.
As a matter of fact, I started with the Val Foix, see, and now he's on the slide.

I was going to ask some more about these. I say we keep trying to get back as early as we can for this history project. Any of the earlier bands that you heard when you were a boy, did you, I suppose you didn't get around so much, that is, even from the outside, did you ever hear any dance halls or any parties?
There was a place on Cleveland, not, I used to, matter of fact, my wife, majority of her people as musicians too.
What was her family name by the way?
Her family name is Bijou, but it was mostly on her momma's side.
There was a famous singer, Esther, I guess it's pronounced Bijou, I forget how it's spelled
now. Probably, but that.
She made records for Oak Cave.
Probably so.
I don't know if she came from here, but she made some records with P. Rowan, so it's possible

that she came from here. Could have been, but the relation of hers is on her mother's side. Yeah. I've been with Johnny Dave. This fellow used to play Sight's iPhone. I can't think of him now. Oh, it's a gob of him. Well, anyhow, they used to rehearse along Calderest Street. Yeah. Well, I used to make it around and listen to them. I used to listen to the Sonny South. He put me on the step. I used to listen to them.
Where was that and what was that?
I don't know. The Sonny South band, Alvin Alcon and quite a few fellas was playing with them.
Oh yeah, I forgot the name.

Well, they used to rehearse across the street from my house. Now, my other brother, one he still plays. He works with Larry every now and then. They used to rehearse about my house. Gene Ware, they used to jam. You know Gene Ware, Harold DeJong, quite a few fellas. Earl Bostic and all of them had rehearsals. At that time, Larry was making up his band. But every Saturday, they used to have a hall on Clearburn and Columbus.
Is that on the river side?
Same side of the Union. Yeah. But between Columbus and La Hoppe.
Somebody said it was about across from the Louisiana funeral.
No, it's in the next block.
The next block.
Down? Yeah, going towards St. Bernard.
Going towards St. Bernard, yeah.

See, the Union sit on this side. Yeah. Sam's side, across the corner, is a big building. Yeah. Well, the fellas used to go, used to play up there on Saturday night. You know, they'd play on the outside on the porch before they go in. Really?
It was right on that corner then?
It's not, it's not exactly on the corner.
No, but near that corner.
Near the corner, yeah.
On the river side.
Matter of fact, the place still there, they made an apartment. Really? I thought, sure, the Union was going to buy it, because it was an ideal place for us. Yeah. Yeah.
I've heard about that place, but I never did see it, and I looked over there, I thought it was across from the Louisiana funeral hall, somebody told me. No.
I guess.
Next block.

I used to, they used to make it their business to get me there to here. Well, it looked like the whole family knew I had loved music, and that's all I could do, so they used to make it possible for me.
Do you remember the name of that hall? Was there a name of it, or a club, or anything?
I think, I ain't sure, man. Let me see, I think they used to call that the Nile Hall. I'm not sure, Bill. I'm not sure. The Nile, what?
Nile Hall, Nile Hall.
I'm not sure, Bill. The Nile, yeah.
Well, we can look it up in some of the old city directories or something. They might even list the fairies.
I really don't know, but you know, I've been out on the road with Ida Cox and all that.
Well, no, I didn't know about Ida Cox.

Yeah. When was that? I didn't know about him out there to get some experience. Yeah. During the, oh, that was, put around, just before he died, I'd say around by 34, 36, probably something like that. During the summer, you know.

Yeah, I'll tell you, one summer, let me think a minute, 1937, I heard Ida Cox in a little theater in St. Louis. I don't remember the street exactly, something like Del Mar, out pretty far from the center of town. Did you ever, remember, travel with her up to St. Louis?
I think I did.
Might be the day, you all heard of the band.
That's around that time, around that time, yeah. Around, what do you say, around, first part of 37 or 37?
This would be in the summer, about June of 37.
Yeah, yeah, because that's the time I went with her during the school time, see, because when I came back then I went with, I went to school a little while and then I went with Joe, Joe Robichoux.
I also remember hearing Ida Cox the last time I heard her, I guess it was during the war, about 1942 or so in Pittsburgh, you wouldn't have been with her.
No, Well after, after I left, matter of fact.
You were pretty young then if you went with her.
I was, yeah, I was.
16 or so, something like that.
Yeah, I was. See, I had went, just like I said, during the summer when school had closed, you know.
Yeah.
Well matter of fact, Bill, I mean, I didn't play with everybody, you know.
Well I suppose a lot of the musicians say that too, they play with, well you can tell even today they keep switching around from one band to another.
Yeah, I played with everybody.
Can you tell us anything more about the Ida Cox troupe? Did she have her whole band with her?

Well she had, at that she had made up a band here. We rehearsed a lot there on the ramp. Right here in town. Ramport in Iran, a place they call the Cotton Club now. At that time we had Bob Ogden, Manuel Cousteau, a boy they call Richard Gray.
What did Cousteau play?
Cousteau was playing trumpet. Yeah, Manuel, Manuel Cousteau. And, let me see. And who was Ogden, what did he play?
Drum, Bob Ogden, Robert Ogden.
Robert Ogden.
Oh really?

Well there's something I want to tell you too Bill. You remember when, I guess you heard about it, well that's before I went out on the road, when Paul Barberan had a cab in town. Well that was the time they had big bands, you know. Yeah. And he made up a big band. And I'll never forget this old, I think it was Will Hudson, the ramming on some kind of serenade. Oh, Moonlight or something? No, no, it wasn't.
No, no, I was just, they don't know it. Yeah.

Well then I, with all the fellas he had in there, well I couldn't cut it, they needed a trombone fellas, I couldn't cut it. I had gotten nervous, you know. Yeah. And that's when he had the big band. But just go with sure, now I'm with him, you know. Yeah. No matter what happened, I'm with him.
Sure, I know you can cut the stuff now from what I've heard of.
I'll never forget that though. I, at that particular time, I guess I just was nervous, you know.

Yeah. I was going to ask some more about the Ida Cox. She just made some records, you know, about the, oh, about the time they made all of those, when Riverside was done. Here, remember in January they cut several bands. And they told me then that they'd just located Ida Cox someplace like up in Kentucky or someplace she...
Well she's from Knoxville, I don't know.

Might have been Tennessee, yeah, maybe it was Tennessee. And she went to New York though and made these records with Coleman Hawkins and it just came out this month. Yeah. It already came out. I didn't hear it. I wondered what kind of songs, when I heard her, she sang just usually blues songs. Yeah. Remember one was a cherry picking blues, she made a record of that. One of these, if you don't, I remember that line, if you don't like my peaches, don't shake my tree and all those.
Yeah, yeah, yeah.
Did she have any other special numbers that you remember?

She did. She did. Well that was, I tell you Bill, that was one reason my dad had told me, you know, go out and get some experience, you know, like for reading. He really wanted me to do it the right way. But after we run down the show, they had music. After we run down, most of them, Miss Cox had music. Well after about a couple of weeks or so, well I mean I was memorizing the music and I mean I didn't need it much. I wasn't advancing at all too much. But she had some pretty nice aramming, but now as far as the name of the tunes, I really don't know. Yeah. She had some nice aramming. Oh yeah, there's another barber from here. Her name was, uh, he was a pianist, but I think he changed his name now. Parnell, Nathaniel Parnell, something like that. He's a pretty good pianist. As a matter of fact, he was an organist in some church uptown.
Oh, wow.
Yeah.
No relation to Alton Parnell and...
No, no, no, I don't think so. No. No relation at all. He's a fine piano player.
So you had about five or so pieces with the...
No, we had more than that Bill.
More than that, huh?
Yeah, we had two trumpet and trombone, three saxophones, and three rhythms.
Oh, big, big group. Yeah.
How you doing?
How you doing? How in? I was just talking about, um, Sprox has a, uh, once toured with Ida Cox, the blues singer, and she got up the band here in New Orleans. Oh, here in New Orleans?
Yeah.
I'll tell you something else too, man. My first job out of town in Bucklewood, Louisiana was with Kid Howard, man. Oh, really?
Yeah.
Yeah, yeah.
When was that, sir?
Oh, I don't know, man. Really, I'd forgotten. I can't keep up. You were a young man, huh?
Yeah.
Is there anything else about the Ida Cox tour? How far did you go, and where, how long did it last?

Well, I went all, all up in Carolina, all up, mostly on the East Coast, Bill. Uh-huh. Mostly all up in Virginia. I think I went all the way to Washington, D.C. Yeah. Because right after that, they got snowbound somewhere, but I was home then, see. Yeah. Because it was time for school open, see, I made it back home, see. As a matter of fact, Emanuel and I made it back home.
Who were your favorite trombone players when you were young? Any, aside from the people you studied with, you must have liked them when you wouldn't

have studied? Well, as a fellow, there's something else I forgot to tell you too. I think he was a great trombone player, but people never talked about him. He was smooth, and he was a fellow who gave me an idea of, you know, peeing up on your ground and playing melody too, was Boots.
Oh yeah.
A very fine trombone man.
I never heard him on trombone, but I heard him on the bass.

See, he used to come by the house and get me. He was playing the jitney down the street or somewhere. And he used to come by the house and get me, because he used to have their music there, you see. Well, Boots used to like to gamble, so he'd come get me and set me down, you know. And I played a couple of hours or so for it. Well, he'll go on the right path street somewhere and get him, come back, send me home in the cab. He used to call the place Budweiser.
Yeah, I heard him there playing bass in 1942, the first time I met him.
Yeah, bass player, but he was a good trombone man.
They said he lost his teeth, I believe, and gave it up. Was that the reason?
Do you know? I don't know Bill, but I know he helped me out a lot too.
Yeah, he was supposed to be a fine musician. I know he was on bass one day.
His brother was too, but if he stays sober enough to do it, he'd be a sport. Sport, yeah. But Boots was a very man, he was smooth man. Yeah, I bet he was fine on trombone.
He was smooth. How was he as far as his tone, loud, soft, or anything? Smooth, nice, nice.
He was pretty tone and all. Tell you the truth, I can imitate him pretty nice, yeah.
Yeah, I wish I'd heard him on trombone, he must have been one of the better.
So you know I heard a lot of them, thought I'd do that, yeah. I can imitate him pretty nice. He was a very fine trombone man. He helped me out a lot.
Did he help you out at home or?
Well no, like you know, on the job. Well I was pretty much advanced when he started coming to get me, you know. Uh-huh. Yeah, you'd, all right.
Were there any other trombones you liked when you were young, even if you didn't hear them so much or study? What you mean hear in?
Just to hear him play, yes. Well I always did like Teagarden. Was he ever around here much?
Did you heard him in person or his records? I heard him in person but not in your own.
Not here.
Not here. Cause somebody told us he was here, Eddie Summers said he studied with Vic Gaspar once.
Well those fellas I never did him.
Took a few lessons from him. I didn't.
See like Vic Gaspar and a lot of those fellas, I never did a chance to really hear him or proud of him or proud of him I didn't even know them.
Yeah, and they were so old they quit I never got to, never even got to meet him.

But just like I said, this New Orleans music, I love him. That's all I know, but it was a good while that I had a chance to really, you know, do it up until Paul gave me the chance, see. Cause all, I would be playing, you know, sort of commercial music.
When did you join Paul's band? Do you remember about what year it was?
Oh about 50, oh about 54 maybe.
And you never recorded though with him?
Yeah, that is all.
Oh that's right, you told me the Southland, one Southland date.
Yeah, that is all.
Nothing else? I was thinking you were-
I made a lot of recording but not this type of music. Outside of Paul and Freddie, just quickly with MGM.
Yeah, with Freddie Coleman.
But a lot of other recordings, you know, with different type of music. Mm-hm. Deer, Paul Gaten.
Some of the blues and rock and roll, everything else like that.
Yeah, everything, yeah, everything. Yeah. So that is why I really would like to get a chance to do that.
Well you might tell us a little bit about some of the original pieces too that you've written. I know the slide, the form, the slide.
Well yeah, well that's the truth, because I have some ideas on that, but for us titles man, I really don't have no idea about what title, name to give them. Yeah.
Mostly things that feature trombone or what?
Yeah, yeah, I like, like Paul said, rags. I like rags, you know. Mm-hm.
I feel it. Yeah.
I like hymns too. I like the rag most of them. I like it.
You were on both the Cook records and that MGM, weren't you, with Freddie Coleman?
Yeah. Well matter of fact, Freddie Coleman, Jack Willis, Sam Dutra, we've been working together off and on for about the last 23, 24 years.
Really? That long was Sam too?
Yeah, you see, because we all have worked with Joe Robichill. Yeah. Then out during the war, well.
Of course, was Sam Dutra in that band that recorded? I forgot.
I don't know. Well, at that time, I think.

he was working with Sidney. But after the war, well, Freddie, Jack, Sam, and I, we got together. Now Bill, this may sound foolish, but before this music came back, we had this little outfit. We had six of us. And we used to play a lot of these New Orleans tunes. And we worked at a place they called the GI Club during the war in Omaha, Nebraska.
Over in Omaha.
And the fella built us up at the Sons of Dixieland, and we didn't take heat to that. But we was playing the tunes.
Yeah, you didn't know all those things.
Well, yeah, we was playing a lot of them. What did he call you? The Sons of Dixieland? Sons of Dixieland, that's right.
And what kind of music were you playing?

We was playing, well, we was playing popular tunes, but we also was playing a lot of tunes like High Society, which the music hadn't got back yet. Remember that, you know, it hadn't got back. We were playing like Sister Kate, High Society, different things. Quite a few of them. And we also, after we left there, we went to Evansville. And we happened to be playing that funny all of these music. Yeah? Yeah. Yeah. We used to call the show bar. Is that all right? It's Sam Wolf. Yeah, that's right. That's one of them things. Now, matter of fact, this is the first time that the Three Horn had a chance to play this type of music on the street. Jack, Sam and I, but we had worked on the street before, but we was playing most of those shows, what you call the ballet club. Yeah, oh yeah.
I remember.
We were strictly, you know, reading and playing a show and playing about three or four tunes. We still would sit down and read, you know. But that was a pretty nice little band at the time.
Is there anything else you can tell us about Sam Duque? We'll finally catch up with him. I guess in an interview. You say you've been working that long, 23 years.
That's how long? Well, I can tell you, I see off and on. Let's say I was about, okay, I'm 41 now. I was about 19, about 19, 18, about 19 years old when I met Sam. I'm glad we're back.
I think a few more things I think we can talk about to fill up some of this. We don't have to fill it all up necessarily. Did you ever know Sam's father? No, no. Old man Sam.
No, I heard of his uncle. Matter of fact, it's a little deal I use now on Sister Kate when I was told his uncle uses it.
On Norrie. Yeah. I liked it, you know. What was that, what part was that? I don't remember. I mean, ever hearing about that. I don't think he ever recorded the…
Well, I don't know if he recorded, but I heard that he used to use it, you know. It's just a B flat, seven chord he run, you know.
I know there's some part in there, they sort of hold some long notes, slide up, can you, can you, can you hum it or sing it in any way?
No better, let me see.
I know it's hard to demonstrate without the trombone, but it's…
Dun, No, I don't really, it, I made it on this, uh, deal with Paul.
Well, it's on the one with Paul. Yeah, yeah. But we'll, if we don't have that, we'll get a copy sooner or later. That record is cut out, but I think I saved one for Tulane on there.
Yeah, yeah, I like that. It's really…
So it was on that Sister Kate, I forget what the Zone went right.

But I don't know if Sam's uncle made it on the record, but Paul told me, you know, as a matter of fact, too. But you know, you like to hear a cat play a thing a long time, you know, and you hear someone else play, you say, well man, so and so done it, you know. Yeah. But it just happened, you keep running the B flat 7 chord, you know, the way you run it.

Yeah, we'll have to get that, because Dutry did record with King Oliver, and that's about the only band he recorded with up north, Joe Oliver and that group. They never made Sister Kate, I'm sure, because I haven't just about every Oliver record made. Did you ever get to hear Dutry in person? Oh, no, no, no. He left almost before you were born, I guess, and went north about that time.
No, I never did hear him, no. I saw some pictures of him. I can see the resemblance of Sam, though.

Yeah, I noticed the resemblance of Sam and his father. Yeah. Here's one picture of the Oliver band over here. Not in there now, let me get it in the back here. Here it is. Look at the door, I don't just light, it burned out a little. It's a little hard to see, I didn't take this cover off. Yeah, I see, I see. Take the cover off, you can see it no easier. They have it in red, they only kept Oliver in the black and white. Yeah, I guess he does, like a little.
Yeah, you see, this is Louie, huh?
Yeah, that's Louie, and then Johnny Dodds and Baby Dodds. That's too bad. Speaking of everything.

Look, one of them married Paul's sister, one of them Dodds married Paul's sister. No, it wasn't in my mother. Was it Kepard? I thought one of these boys, Johnny Dodds or something, I thought one of them.

No, I think it was Jimmy Noon, not Kepard, Jimmy Noon. Oh, Jimmy Noon? Jimmy Noon, that's who it was. Who was that on base, Bill? Bill Johnson, we've been trying to find him. He's over probably in San Antonio now. He's about 90 years old, he would be. He was 75 when I saw him. He's still living? He was two years ago. Did you find out from Don Albert? I asked him, he didn't know him. He said he's never seen him over there.
Well, they have another drummer over there from here. Old fellow in San Antonio.
Did you see Don Albert, I guess?
Well, yeah, well, he stayed right around the corner from the house. We worked for him when we had Freddie band too.
Oh, over in San Antonio?
Yeah.
You were over there? The whole Freddie Coleman band? Yeah. I didn't know they went over there.
Oh man, we went, we went, quite a few places. We had a pretty nice little band. Not to say our band was at the Mardi Grimes.
Yeah.
Different band. Different group there.

Yeah, matter of fact, we had a nice little arrangement, you know. One second, let me look up this. Paul Barban record. Did you? This is Bob Thomas was on trombone on this one. Yeah, yeah, yeah. And they didn't play any of your numbers either, I guess. No, no, no. First choice, Scream in the Blues, a couple of things that Paul... First choice, Scream in the Blues, a couple of things that Paul... First choice, that's John Bruins, a picket, that's his tune. Yeah.

And a couple of Paul's, a couple of Paul's, a couple of things that Paul... ...a couple of Paul's, a couple of Paul's, a couple of Paul's, a couple of Paul's. Yeah. Yeah. Alright, I'll take a look up this Paul Barban record.

Alright, I'll take a look up this Paul Barban record. I knew somebody else beside that. Did he do? This is Bob Thomas was on trombone on this one. Yeah, yeah, yeah. And they didn't play any of your numbers either, I guess. No, no, no. First choice, Scream in the Blues, a couple of things that Paul... First choice, that's John Bruins, a picket, that's his tune. A couple of Paul's second line. Yeah. Somehow I had you mixed up that you might have been on there.
No. That's a good tune, that second line. I think I like it better than Spoonin' Street.
They made those in New York too, I guess, on one of their trips. Did you ever get to New York and Chicago much?
Well, I worked at the Jazz Limited about five months.
Oh, that's right. I remember you told me.
Yeah. I played in New York quite a bit. Lee Allen, rock and roll band, anything. I've been all over Bill, but California.
Haven't been all over?
I stayed down in Cuba six weeks with Joe Rubischoff. Well I stayed eight weeks in Canada with Paul. I stayed four weeks in Montreal with Lee Allen. I've been around.

Are there any other favorite trombone players that you've heard? Especially some of the old timers from here that you might, that you could tell something about their style and all too. Like you were talking about some of the other fellas.

Well, that's one man I had a chance to hear more. Now outside my friend Clement and I, we used to study together. But we played with Joe Rubischoff together. And a lot of times when we was younger, well if we played trombone on the job, well I may play piano or bass. Did you have a piano at home to practice on? Not now. I mean when you were a boy. I did, yeah. I had a piano. Matter of fact I got the piano, I was supposed to give him exercise, you know. You had the pump then, huh? Yeah, yeah. Pump.
Well that was a pretty good idea. Yeah, that's a good idea. Yeah.
You know, you know, I come along with stuff I come a long way.
Yeah, I imagine so. How old were you when you had bullying all night?
Thirteen months old. Fell down.
Really? Just a baby?
Yeah, I was walking, fell down the back step. There were three kids in the blockhead. I come out bed and all of them.
Yeah, you were lucky to get through as good as you did. Now they have all those shots and things.
Oh yeah, they got all that.
I was going to ask some more about the New Orleans style. It was very nice to be retelling about that melody. Like your father taught you about it. The melody should always be heard.
Yeah, that's right.
A lot of the fellows that told us that. I find out.
I mean, to hold a legit job, if that's going on all the time, you may hold that job a good while. You know, keep that melody going.

Is there anything else about the style of playing trombone? Because actually, maybe people from away from here, like I was born up north, we noticed that the bands from New Orleans always seem to have a better rhythm and a better beat. And somehow, to me, it's a lot better music than most of the other bands that developed up north. Is there anything about the trombone style that you've-

Well, I'll tell you one thing, I noticed, I mean, like this type of music. I mean, the fellows, they used more pedal notes than a lot of the other fellows. And it just, I don't know, it looked like New Orleans just got something different. And I'll tell you this, Bill, a little experience that I had in Washington, New York, Chicago. I had a chance, you know, was off and fellows come to get me for a gig, you know. And, well, I went to work with them. But somehow or another, it don't look like they get together fast like we do. You know, if you take about five or six men in the yard, and after that they tune up and play about fifteen or twenty minutes, it sounds like they're organized.
Yeah, that's what I always noticed too, that they seem to play together. I noticed that now, yeah, that's for sure. They know how to work together.
I'm not saying the other fellows, not musicians, I'm not speaking about their ability.
No, some of them can get all over their horns and everything fast.
But I mean they're just saying, well, you know, like we do, well we get on the phone and say, so you're working in that? Okay, man, okay. In about fifteen minutes.
Yeah, you've got a band that's playing. We've got a band.
After we find out what the people want, probably we may not be able to play all the tunes that
they want.
Yeah, sure. It's a bit of satisfying. That's one thing.
Yeah, I think so too, that's one of the main things that the- Now what it is, I don't know.
I don't know what it is.

Yeah. Is there anything about the way you play trombone, or all of the fellas, I mean the whole city, the way they play trombone, that you notice is distinctive, that is more slides, or maybe used more as a rhythm. The old timers talk about vamping, you know, sort of like playing a bass part, you know, filling in that way.

Well I had looked at some old music back and somehow or another that's the way they used to write it. You know, they vamp, they play the bass part, I might play the first, third and fifth, or wholesome notes. But that had been changed.
Yeah, of course as they say nowadays they play more like trumpet parts sometimes. Yeah.

Well I tell you for one reason, it's like out on the street, I mean, they had to do something because the music would be coming up so fast that, you know, it would be hard on the trumpet place. So, trombone, prayer, you know. So, now you take, you take, if you take some of the hymns that they play, I mean the vamp is right. It fits, it fits, the vamp fits, that's for sure. Because it would sound bad, you know, trying to put some other things in there. The vamp really fits. A lot of the new ones in tune that you can't get away from vamping.
What do you mean exactly by that term in vamping? Of course the old sheet music, remember they used to always say vamp till ready, and the pianist would sort of chord along.
Well all I can understand about vamping really is just play something, after you done heard heard the melody, you know, playing the key out.
Sort of filling in the cards, the notes of the cards.
Does it mean more of a rhythm part?
Yeah, it means, it
still like the dead.

tell you vamp out. Suppose you sing it and it tell you vamp out. They say vamp out, well you'll either make a B flat or a G minor or a C7 or a F7. But you just keep that no matter what you do. I'm vamping on out. I just use that as a.
I understand myself what you mean by I just wondering what sort of your definition of the vamping style is because a lot of people. Well that's the idea that I got you know

because after all you know I come find them fellas saying them things you know. They didn't take time out to really find out what happened so I just got on with them with my horn. I said that's the best way to do that you know. I mean it's what you want man. Just get with them. That's all. I think that's really jazz myself. Yeah I think so. Yeah. Just get with them. Which way you going I'm going that way too. I think they come out real good sometimes.

Yeah that's right. Yeah. I was going to ask a little bit more about the numbers when you write them. Do you sort of improvise them first then you hear them in your head first and then write them down or do you just get a piece of paper and start working from the paper? What do you do when you write them?

I don't practice that too much but I always like to fool around with the piano and that's the way I get it. Work it out on the piano. I hear it you know. Yeah sure you have to hear it. As a matter of fact I had man one day one evening I was sleeping before the gig man I had a good melody there man. And by not having a piano it stayed with me all that night till I got to work man. I got to work I lost it.
You lost the ball already huh? Lost it. I'm just wondering if you'd work them out on your trombone?

Oh well I didn't do that. Yeah I didn't do that. You had her on the piano if you did. Well without I already have the piano I mean that's just my system. I don't know it ain't right. That's right for me. But so anything at all. Well I can write the melody and also write the chord at the same time. Yeah. So then after I get the melody down if I want to change the chord well I you know. You can talk. Yep.
You say you don't, some of your songs you don't even have titles for yet.

Well I don't have too many of them. About two or three of them. And I got the other two I have in mind I don't have no title for them. Mm-hmm. Now Paul and I got to get on the slide for a slide because when I got with them at the Mardi Gras a lot of people used to ask for
Ur's trombone. Oh yeah. Ur's Creole trombone.

Well you know out there on the street I mean take a tune like Ur's Creole trombone. Well I mean you got to feel them things you know. Yeah just start to know trick things that he does. Yeah well I mean he can do more justice with it than uh than anyone else. Well you didn't have no time to rehearsal. And you know the man don't want no music sitting up there. Yeah. So we got together and said well we're going to get the tune. So we Paul had a pretty good idea on regs. Mm-hmm. So we got together and well I feel that. Yeah it's a good number. Yeah. Yeah I feel that. I didn't really feel that. But now I, now matter of fact I bought the music to uh uh Ur's trombone. Oh I didn't know it was published that. Yeah I got it. I got a stock on it.
I didn't even know. I knew he had the uh Musgrave Rambles Savoy Blues published. I didn't know that.
And it come out. Yeah. Yeah he got that. He got the stock on it.
It's nice. Did you ever get to hear Ur's in person?
Never did. Never did see him. Really?

Uh-uh. He was down here about four almost more like six years ago. I think he went through here when his sister died and was here a couple of days is all. But hardly anybody saw him that I've taught. Never did see him Bill. We interviewed him uh two years ago in California. Yeah. Professor Minetta was out there with him.
That's a good. I love him man. He's nice. Professor Minetta. He's taught a lot of musicians around here. Yeah I like him. Nice fella.

Now I never get a chance to hear the issues. Yeah, or he was around Chicago a lot. I heard him in late days only from 1940. I met him when I was in California in 1940. He was playing bass then. Started giving up trombone and he came back a couple years later on trombone.
Well look, the same they do all the trombone play double on bass.
Yeah, I guess it's an easy instrument and a way to do both in the bass.
Looks like they lead the trombone on the bass but I had the bass a little bit before I had the trombone.
The trombone. You still play bass ever? I know it Bill. I can sit down and read a little bit, you know, pretty good. No practice it.
Bill? Yeah.

Did you ever play the bass tuba? No, no Bill. Just the string bass. When you played the bass in the old days when you were young and started on the did you bow a good deal or just pick most of the time?
Well no, now I see, now I'm glad you see that. That's the honest way my dad could play. With the bow? With the bow.
That's what I hear. The old timers always said they played the bow a lot. You don't see that
and hear it anymore now. No, he used to bow. But I just fool around with it, you know. Because I remember I'd be fooling around with it. He used to say, oh, quit picking that thing man.
Boy, quit picking. Is he a pretty strict musician? Did he help you on things or? Well, some of those old timers they tell you. I'll tell you one thing about it though Bill.

I'm glad he done it. Like if you know like a kid he'd be trying to blow something on his own like a poplar tune or something like that. But when I picked up my horn, he wanted me to start my lesson off first. Then after I remember my lesson off a while, well he didn't care what I do after that. Used to see that when I got in me so that's what I always did too. And he didn't know how to read the music, but he knew what was supposed to happen, you know.
Yeah.

So that is the same thing, what I'm doing with my kid. See, I know it's time coming that you have to know both of the horns, the valve and the slide. So I had him to start off on the valve first. Now he practiced, after Auburn he practiced a while with the slide then and the valve. Practiced both of them.
Well, I guess you never, when you were young you didn't use the valve, huh?
Oh no, no. I just got the valve, well after, oh about five or six years ago.

Did you ever hear any of the dance artists in the old days when they still used the valve? No, no. Like Old Man Carnish and some of those that used it when they, I guess Frankie. No, I don't know nothing about that. Ever hear Frankie Doosen play? No. Because that's before your time. Although he should have been around in the 20s, but you would have been pretty young.
Oh no, I don't know.
Did you ever hear of Morris French, who was one of the old timers, but he's up around, I don't know whether it's Baton Rouge or farther south.
That's Albert French uncle, no? Yes. No, Bill, I never heard.
Or he's up around Laplace or someplace up there. Yeah.

But you know at one time, I mean during the time I was coming up, you know it was pretty hard for Trumont Player to get a job, you know. And if I wouldn't have went with Joe Robichill, Clement and I, we wouldn't, I guess probably wouldn't be playing that music. Mm-hmm.
What was the trouble? They used mostly smaller bands or used all saxes? Saxophone, you know saxophone was popular. Yeah, that's his famous apartment.
So that's why I was doubling on piano and things like that. Yeah. But I never just put the horn on. Yeah. But trombone was pretty hard to get a gig on.
Yeah, I heard.
Now they're using it in everything. If you notice it, trombone is being used now, a lot, in rock and roll.
Yeah, they've been featuring in there. Of course all of those, the modern bop players, they too began using a lot like that. Yeah.
Yeah, they used a lot.
Those J and K things, you know where they used trombones.

Oh yeah, well I knew J.J. Yeah. Matter of fact, well yeah, matter of fact when Sam, Jack, Clement, some other fellows from here, they was playing with Fed Terrell. Remember Fed Terrell? After he left Randy Crick, well they had formed up a band. Oh yeah. Him and Clines Love. Well J.J., he went over to Benny Carter's band, so I went on and we're taking his place, you see. But trombone is being used a lot man, because I make quite a few recordings at times on the rock and roll deal. They use a lot.

Is there anything else about your life, or the different bands you've played with, or the men you've heard or worked with? Well I'll tell you. You're going to be off, we have three or four more minutes on here, we don't have to come up.

Well I got, I got to tell you. Okay. I done worked, I done worked with Sidney Dazman, Joe Rubenshill, Celestine, quite a few other fellows, Kid Howard, John Lewis, Paul Barberman, and the kids were gigging with, I didn't gig with most everybody in the world. Everybody that I knew of, and still gigging with a lot of the younger fellows. And practically I didn't work every house on Bourbon Street.
Oh I suppose. Did you ever play with any brass band even for concert purposes or anything like the tour?

No Bill, I always wanted to, but it never to get a chance. I thought I had a chance one time when I gave a fellow out there, Joe Pazzo, I said, why don't you, maybe the city might be able to do something for y'all, you know. Yeah. And I said they got a fireman band, police band, might be able to do something. Well he was trying, this fellow Pazzo. Yeah, Willie. Willie, Willie.
Willie Pazzo.
Well he was trying to rig up something and then materialize.
You see in the, during the Depression they had that great big brass band, the WPA band. Oh yeah, well yeah, well. That was before your time almost.
I remember that because they used to come in the neutral ground on Seminar Street. Mm-hmm. I remember that.
You never did play with them then? No. You were probably 20 years old then.
No, but I had no worries then. Yeah.
Yeah, yeah.
I was looking up on the wrist and take care of me then. Yeah.
Did you ever play trumpet or clarinet or anything, any other smaller instruments? No.
No Bill, that's...
How did you happen to like trombone? I mean not that it needs any explanation or reason.
I don't know Bill.
Is there any special reason why you like trombone, why you finally settled on that? It's a wonderful instrument and then of course you can say that all of them.
I had a, I'll tell you the truth Bill, I had a tough pick between them drums and the trombone. Really? But when we was with Freddie and also Joe Rubin, she always had a chance to play some drums.
You would sit in front of them and do that?

Oh yeah, all the time. See then when we had Freddie, a little band, Freddie used to do a hack or so, you know, used to play the drums. I didn't know that. Yeah. I still play them, but I'm pretty much on the drum. But I had a kind of tough pick there. Yeah. But what knocked it out was I wasn't able to carry all that stuff.
Oh yeah, that would make it. Yeah.
Yeah, that was the marrying deal. They went to string bass. That cut me out too, see? It's a tough thing for anybody. And the piano, I just didn't like it too much. Just enough to do what I want.
Just enough to accompany people and help out.
Yeah, do it, you know, to play something for myself or I want to line and stuff like that.
Is there any other thing about trombone that you can think of, the distinct style that they have here? Do you think they do more sliding and all, or here than they would do?

Well, with this type of, with this type. A Pixie Land type of thing? Yeah. But uh, this, yeah, with this type, I'll tell you the truth, this, these fellas here, I think the only fellas really could play like that. With this New Orleans type of thing.
Yeah, that's the only ones I've heard really good.

But as far as playing like, uh, you know, the communication of music now is, with records is so fast now. I mean, you can copy, if you've got any kind of knowledge of music, you can copy who you want. Yeah. Sound like you, you know, like you want to. Yeah. But as they knew all anything, man, that's, that's it.
Mm-hmm.
And the fellas are dying out.
Yeah. The old timers, the old style is going.
They're going.
Or he's still going. There's a piece in the paper about him just two days ago. You happen to see that he's moving down to Los Angeles, but he's still active.
Yeah, well that's good.
He's about 76 years old, so.
But I got, now I'm, I got a pretty good idea, you know, just how that thing goes. I got a good idea how it's supposed to go. Just listen to records, you know.
Yeah, sure.
I was small.
I remember, I remember a lot. So, uh, by the way, in the street bands, did you hear many parades or see many of them, even if they went by your house when you were a kid?

Can you remember many? Yeah, yeah, yeah. Plenty of advertising, you know, who'd be playing on them, I know. Like my oldest brother, if he'd be playing on the advertising, quite natural, the fellas always going to pass around their house.
They'll be on the Reagans, you mean?
Yeah, yeah. Yeah, I remember that. I remember that good. I didn't miss nothing. Anytime it got around music close to the house, I didn't miss nothing.
You'd get there somehow.
Just like I said, I used to rehearse about my house a lot. Somewhere in the block, somebody was rehearsing. I didn't miss nothing when it was close.
People said there was more music in those days. Can you remember, within your memory, was there more bands working and more music all over town then?
Well, I tell you a minute. I'm sorry. I'm sorry. I'm sorry. I'm sorry. I'm sorry.
At the time when I was a teenager there was more live music, man, because people give parties, man. When we was kids we'd hire a little band, they'd play plenty of little parties, man.
Yeah, I've heard about that too, long parties and fish fries and everything of that kind.
And all up in here, man, work for down, quarter of the night, down, that was good money, I mean, you know.
During the depression, yeah.
I mean, but that was good, like, I'm going to school and all that, man, you know, that's pretty nice, you know. Yeah, I'm pretty nice.

Where did you finish your students, you were at the Carpets Christy or how many? I went to Tech Grid and I went to Zerber for two years. So you had the Xavier, I didn't know you went to college there. No. When you mentioned going to, going out to the summer.
Well, Carpets Christy at that time had up to 8th grade, I think they got up to 9th now.
Yeah, I never did notice how it was organized there. They still put on their parade there every spring.
Yeah, yeah, that's coming up again.
They still had the school band there, do you know?
I don't know, Bill. I don't know, to tell you the truth. I mean, that I remember, because I'm born and raised right up there. I'm pretty, you know, a member of the church.
They usually have a...
But I think the best band ever they had, not because I was there, I mean, it was right in the way we were.
I can believe that too. Yeah. They usually have some uniform band. I know John Brunish's boy played the parade a couple years ago. Oh, that was Xavier.
That was Xavier's band. Was that the Xavier band? Yeah, that's the college band. Was that the college band?
Well, I thought maybe it was the high school band.
No, that's Xavier. Yeah, yeah, the high school band. That's right. I must think about, because I know little John was going to college.
Yeah, because I thought he was... The high school band. At that time he was in high school.
Yeah, yeah, that's Xavier high school.
About 17, 16.
Yeah, see when you leave Carpet Christie, well you go there, you know.
Does Xavier have their high school out there on Washington, the same place as they call
Asia? No, that's the college. No, Xavier high school is up Magazine.

Oh yeah, sure, then I know that place. That's Xavier there, that's right. That's right high school. That's right. The kids from downtown go all the way up there then. Yeah, well then where else do they go? Yeah, I guess then.
Now they got St. Augustine, now they got a good band there. They got a good band. Where is that now?
St. Augustine that's on London.
Oh yeah, I know that. They got a good band there.
Yeah, out near where Lawrence Barretta used to live down there. Yeah, my kids be going there this year.
Yeah, sure, I know now where they are.
They got a good band there. Well, there's still a half a minute, anything else that you want to add before we...
Well, the only thing I'd say I'd give credit to Paul Barber when I get me this, this deal, something that I would always like to do, you know.

He's a nice fella. Oh, we might ask this for a minute, I know Paul would be one of your favorite drummers and you mentioned a few others that you've worked with too. Are there any other drummers that you liked when you were a kid and young coming up that impressed you, especially some of the old timers, you know, I mean, maybe... Well, yeah. Did you ever hear old man Cottrell? No, no, no, no.
He was in a P. Rome's band.

No, no, I don't remember that. But I'll tell you a fella I used to like, Joe Relic. Oh, yeah. But this is what I want to tell you before I go. This is one thing I remember my daddy told me too, and I do that.

If you're going to learn music, do it just like anything else. If you was a carpenter you couldn't tell me you couldn't build a two-story house. You couldn't build just one story. So if you're going to play music, try to play all type of music if you've got to make a living out. And I never will forget that. So that's why, I mean, I try to play all the music. I mean, I love the New Orleans music, but sometimes I can't make a living out. And that's all I can do is play the music.

I know down here though, the dancers, they always, that impressed me too when I first came down, they always played waltzes and other kinds of pieces. Up, say in New York, if you'd ask Eddie Conner or somebody to play a waltz, they'd be insulted. They'd say, get out of here, this is a jazz band. But down here they play all the guys. That's one thing you've got to give to the New Orleans musicians.
They try to satisfy, you know, the guests, you know.
Yeah, I've always noticed that too as being one of the main features of the bands here.
What type of music come up now, I try to get a little bit of it, learn a little bit of it, make it out. Your father actually impressed you with that.
He really did.
That's one thing I never will forget. Very interesting, isn't it? Yeah. I mean, you know, they got some fellas, they'll cater to just one type of music.
Yeah.

Well, if you're cater to one type of music, it's all right if that's your sideline, but if you're going to make a living out of it, well, you've got to get with everything. Yeah, sure, that's right. Music is music with me. Yeah. But you've got something you like, you know.
Well, I guess that's about the end of the tape here. stuff

segments.chapter: Family and early childhood
segments.title: Name, nickname and birth in the 7th Ward
segments.summary: Joseph gives his full name (Waldren Clement Joseph), says musicians call him Frog, and gives his 1919 birth in the 7th Ward.

segments.chapter: Family and early childhood
segments.title: Musical family: father a bass player, brothers
segments.summary: He describes his father's string bass, his drummer and singer brothers, being the youngest, and his father's death when he was about seventeen.

segments.chapter: Family and early childhood
segments.title: Polio, instruments in the house, first drums at school
segments.summary: Braced from polio, he was given instruments at home; drums came first, taught by Sister Cyril, and he played in the school band.

segments.chapter: Family and early childhood
segments.title: Father's life, brother who knows jazz history, his address
segments.summary: Joseph knows little of his father's early life; he points to his brother as a knowledgeable source and gives his address, and recalls his father leaving instruments out for the children.

segments.chapter: Learning drums and trombone
segments.title: Drum sets and group instruction at school
segments.summary: He used his oldest brother's drum set and the school's drums, learning in group lessons and reading music.

segments.chapter: Learning drums and trombone
segments.title: Trombone teachers: Gene Ware, Pinchback Tureaud, Eddie Pearson
segments.summary: His first trombone teacher was Gene Ware, followed by lessons with Pinchback Tureaud and Eddie Pearson while still playing drums in the school band.

segments.chapter: Learning drums and trombone
segments.title: Starting drums at seven, school band, Manuel Cruz and piano gigs
segments.summary: He began drums around age seven, joined the school band at ten, and played piano on gigs with Manuel Cruz while trombone was still not in demand.

segments.chapter: Learning drums and trombone
segments.title: Switching to trombone, a gig without a trumpet, credit to Paul Barbarin
segments.summary: He switched to trombone at 15-16, recalls a trumpetless gig with a tuba, stresses always playing the melody, and credits Paul Barbarin for bringing him into New Orleans jazz.

segments.chapter: Learning drums and trombone
segments.title: Father's name and bands, borrowed bass, playing all instruments
segments.summary: He gives his father's name as Arthur Joseph, names someone who knew his father, and explains he practised bass, trombone and others at once.

segments.chapter: Learning drums and trombone
segments.title: Gene Ware: Robichaux trombonist and arranger
segments.summary: Joseph says Gene Ware played with Robichaux and others, recorded in the early thirties and was a good arranger who helped him.

segments.chapter: Learning drums and trombone
segments.title: The first trombone method book
segments.summary: They try to pin down the name of his first method book, 'White Excelsior', and he mentions starting on valve trombone.

segments.chapter: Neighborhood halls and the Ida Cox tour
segments.title: His wife's musical family
segments.summary: Asked about early bands he heard, he mentions his wife's family, the Bijou name, and her mother's musical relatives.

segments.chapter: Neighborhood halls and the Ida Cox tour
segments.title: Rehearsals near his house and a hall near the Union
segments.summary: Bands including Sonny South's rehearsed across from his house, and musicians played Saturday dances at a hall near the Musicians' Union, possibly called the Nile Hall.

segments.chapter: Neighborhood halls and the Ida Cox tour
segments.title: Joining Ida Cox's tour at sixteen
segments.summary: Joseph recalls going on the road with Ida Cox in a school summer around 1937, before he joined Joe Robichaux, and says he played with everybody.

segments.chapter: Neighborhood halls and the Ida Cox tour
segments.title: Ida Cox's New Orleans band: Ogden, Manuel Cousteau, Richard Gray
segments.summary: The band Cox assembled in New Orleans rehearsed locally; Joseph names the drummer Bob Ogden, trumpeter Manuel Cousteau and Richard Gray.

segments.chapter: Neighborhood halls and the Ida Cox tour
segments.title: Nervous in Paul Barbarin's big band
segments.summary: He recalls that when Paul Barbarin formed a big band he was too nervous to cut the trombone parts, but remains loyal to him.

segments.chapter: Neighborhood halls and the Ida Cox tour
segments.title: Ida Cox's records, repertoire and big band
segments.summary: They discuss Ida Cox's blues and recent records; Joseph says the job taught him reading, the band had two trumpets, trombone, three saxes and three rhythm, and a pianist from New Orleans.

segments.chapter: Neighborhood halls and the Ida Cox tour
segments.title: Visitor joins; first out-of-town job with Kid Howard
segments.summary: A visitor arrives; Joseph says his first out-of-town job, in Bucklewood, Louisiana, was with Kid Howard.

segments.chapter: Neighborhood halls and the Ida Cox tour
segments.title: Route of the Ida Cox tour up the East Coast
segments.summary: The tour went through the Carolinas and Virginia, perhaps to Washington, ending when school reopened.

segments.chapter: Trombone influences
segments.title: Boots, the smooth trombonist turned bassist
segments.summary: Joseph praises Boots as a fine, smooth trombonist who played melody, used to fetch him for jobs, and helped him; Russell only heard him on bass.

segments.chapter: Trombone influences
segments.title: Other trombonists he admired: Teagarden, Vic Gaspar
segments.summary: He always liked Jack Teagarden but never heard him locally, and never heard older players such as Vic Gaspar.

segments.chapter: Barbarin band and postwar groups
segments.title: Joining Barbarin's band and his recordings
segments.summary: He joined Paul Barbarin's band around 1954, made one Southland date, and many other recordings in other styles.

segments.chapter: Barbarin band and postwar groups
segments.title: His own compositions and fondness for rags
segments.summary: Joseph has ideas for original pieces but no titles; he likes rags and hymns.

segments.chapter: Barbarin band and postwar groups
segments.title: Freddie Kohlman, Jack Willis and Sam Dutrey; the Omaha GI club
segments.summary: He has worked on and off with Freddie, Jack and Sam for over twenty years, from Robichaux days to a wartime little band in Omaha and Evansville.

segments.chapter: Barbarin band and postwar groups
segments.title: Sam Dutrey's uncle and the Sister Kate trombone figure
segments.summary: Joseph recalls meeting Sam at about 19 and a B-flat seventh figure on Sister Kate attributed to Sam's uncle, which he plays on the record with Paul.

segments.chapter: Barbarin band and postwar groups
segments.title: Oliver band photo, the Dodds and Bill Johnson
segments.summary: Looking at a photo of King Oliver's band, they discuss Dutrey, the Dodds family and the search for Bill Johnson in San Antonio.

segments.chapter: Barbarin band and postwar groups
segments.title: Playing for Don Albert in San Antonio; a Barbarin record
segments.summary: Joseph says Freddie's band worked in San Antonio for Don Albert, and they look at a Barbarin record without him.

segments.chapter: Barbarin band and postwar groups
segments.title: Travels: Jazz Limited, New York, Cuba, Canada
segments.summary: He worked five months at Jazz Limited and travelled to Cuba, Canada and Montreal with various leaders.

segments.chapter: Barbarin band and postwar groups
segments.title: Studying with Clement and playing piano and bass on jobs
segments.summary: He and his friend Clement studied together and worked with Robichaux, swapping trombone and piano or bass, with a pedal piano at home.

segments.chapter: Barbarin band and postwar groups
segments.title: Polio at thirteen months
segments.summary: He fell down the back steps at thirteen months and was ill, and Russell notes children now get shots.

segments.chapter: New Orleans trombone style and composing
segments.title: Why New Orleans bands play together fast
segments.summary: They discuss keeping the melody heard, pedal notes, and how New Orleans musicians form a band quickly, unlike players in other cities.

segments.chapter: New Orleans trombone style and composing
segments.title: Vamping on the trombone
segments.summary: Joseph and Russell try to define vamping: trombone playing bass-like parts and harmony in street music, and his approach of getting with the band.

segments.chapter: New Orleans trombone style and composing
segments.title: How he writes tunes at the piano
segments.summary: He composes at the piano, writes melody and chords together, lost a melody once, and has few titles.

segments.chapter: New Orleans trombone style and composing
segments.title: Ory's Creole Trombone at Mardi Gras
segments.summary: With Paul he plays Ory's Creole Trombone on the street; he bought the music, never saw Ory, and Russell recalls interviewing him in California.

segments.chapter: New Orleans trombone style and composing
segments.title: Trombonists doubling on bass
segments.summary: He notes trombonists often double on bass, played string bass before trombone, and never played bass tuba.

segments.chapter: New Orleans trombone style and composing
segments.title: Father bowing the bass and insisting on lessons first
segments.summary: His father bowed the bass and insisted on lessons before playing popular tunes; Joseph teaches his own son valve and slide, and only took up valve trombone recently.

segments.chapter: New Orleans trombone style and composing
segments.title: Early valve trombone players
segments.summary: Russell asks about valve trombonists such as Frankie Dusen and Morris French; Joseph never heard them.

segments.chapter: Career, brass bands and choice of instrument
segments.title: Trombone gigs hard to get; J.J. Johnson and Fed Terrell
segments.summary: Trombone was hard to book when he was coming up, so he doubled on piano; he recalls replacing J.J. Johnson in a Fed Terrell band and trombone's rise in rock and roll.

segments.chapter: Career, brass bands and choice of instrument
segments.title: Leaders he has worked with
segments.summary: He lists Sidney Desvigne, Robichaux, Celestine, Kid Howard, Barbarin and others, and says he worked nearly every Bourbon Street house.

segments.chapter: Career, brass bands and choice of instrument
segments.title: No brass band experience; the WPA band
segments.summary: He never played in a brass band though he suggested one to Willie Pajeaud, and remembers the WPA band.

segments.chapter: Career, brass bands and choice of instrument
segments.title: Why trombone over drums, bass and piano
segments.summary: He nearly chose drums but could not carry them, found bass and piano less appealing, and settled on trombone.

segments.chapter: Career, brass bands and choice of instrument
segments.title: New Orleans style and the old timers dying out
segments.summary: Only New Orleans players really play this style; records let anyone copy, and the old musicians are dying out.

segments.chapter: Music scene, school and father's advice
segments.title: Parades and rehearsals near his boyhood home
segments.summary: He saw advertising wagons and parades and rehearsals close to his house and missed none of them.

segments.chapter: Music scene, school and father's advice
segments.title: More live music and parties in his teens
segments.summary: There was more live music when he was a teenager, with house parties and fish fries paying good money during the Depression.

segments.chapter: Music scene, school and father's advice
segments.title: Carpet Christie, Xavier and school bands
segments.summary: They compare school bands at Carpet Christie, Xavier high school and college, and St. Augustine.

segments.chapter: Music scene, school and father's advice
segments.title: Credit to Paul Barbarin and favourite drummers
segments.summary: He again credits Paul Barbarin, and names Joe Relic as a drummer he liked.

segments.chapter: Music scene, school and father's advice
segments.title: Father's advice: play all types of music
segments.summary: His father told him to learn all kinds of music in order to make a living, and Russell contrasts New Orleans bands with northern ones.

segments.chapter: Music scene, school and father's advice
segments.title: End of the tape
segments.summary: Russell closes the tape.
